Leopard
LEP-erd
noun
From the Latin leopardus, compounded of leo, a lion, and pardus, a panther, from the old notion that the beast was a cross of the two; rendering the Hebrew namer, a spotted beast of prey, the swift and dappled hunter of the hills of Canaan.

Biblical Definition

The leopard is the spotted beast of prey, swift, silent and marked for life. Scripture names it for three things: its speed, its lying in wait, and above all its spots. Habakkuk sets the Chaldean cavalry beside it — horses “swifter than the leopards” (Hab 1:8); Daniel sees the third kingdom as a leopard with four wings and four heads, dominion given to it (Dan 7:6), speed itself made an empire. But the verse that carries the doctrine is Jeremiah’s: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil” (Jer 13:23). The prophet is not moralising. He is stating an impossibility and drawing a conclusion from it. A man habituated in sin can no more reform himself than the beast can wash out its markings, for the marking is not on him but in him. This is the bondage of the will in a single image: the sinner does exactly what he wants, and what he wants is the trouble. Nothing but a new nature will serve, which is why regeneration is a birth and not a resolution. And Scripture will not leave the leopard under the curse. In the kingdom of the Branch, “the leopard shall lie down with the kid” (Isa 11:6) — the spots unchanged, the ferocity gone, because the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD.

Webster 1828 Definition

A fierce spotted beast of prey; in Scripture the emblem of swiftness in judgment and of a nature that cannot change itself.

expand to see more

LEOPARD, a rapacious quadruped of the cat kind, with a spotted skin.

From the Latin leo, a lion, and pardus, a panther.

Renders the Hebrew namer, the dappled hunter of the hills.

Proverbial for what cannot be altered: “or the leopard his spots” (Jer 13:23).

A figure of swift conquest in prophecy (Dan 7:6; Hab 1:8).

Key Scripture

Jer 13:23 — "Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil."

Isa 11:6 — "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them."

Jer 5:6 — "Wherefore a lion out of the forest shall slay them, and a wolf of the evenings shall spoil them, a leopard shall watch over their cities: every one that goeth out thence shall be torn in pieces: because their transgressions are many, and their backslidings are increased."

Hab 1:8 — "Their horses also are swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves: and their horsemen shall spread themselves, and their horsemen shall come from far; they shall fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat."

Modern Corruption

Jer 13:23 is quoted as a shrug — people never change — when the verse is a diagnosis whose only cure is the new birth.

expand to see more

The leopard’s spots have become a proverb of fatalism. A man is written off, a marriage abandoned, a wayward son given up, and the verse is quoted over the wreckage as though Jeremiah had taught that human nature is fixed and that is the end of the matter. That is half the verse and none of its purpose. Jeremiah is preaching to a people who supposed a little reform would restore them, and he takes away the ladder: you who are accustomed to do evil can no more do good by resolving to than the beast can rub off its markings. The point of an impossibility in Scripture is never resignation. It is to drive the hearer off his own resources and onto God, who does impossible things.

So the verse that seems to close the door is the very one that names where the door is. If the spots cannot be changed from without, the creature must be changed from within — and that is precisely what the Lord promises through the same prophet, a new heart and His law written on the inward parts, and through Ezekiel a heart of flesh for a heart of stone, and through our Lord to Nicodemus a birth from above. Regeneration is not the sinner scrubbing at his skin; it is God giving him a new nature, out of which new doing comes. Isa 11:6 is the picture of the end of it: the leopard still spotted, lying down beside the kid, its whole ferocity taken away by the King who reigns.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The spotted hunter — swift in prophecy, and the standing emblem of a nature no man can alter in himself.

expand to see more

Leopard — Latin leopardus, from leo (lion) and pardus (panther).

Hebrew namer, a spotted beast of prey known in the hills of Canaan.

Jer 13:23 makes the unchangeable spots the figure of habituated sin.

Dan 7:6 and Hab 1:8 use the leopard for the speed of conquering empires; Jer 5:6 for judgment lying in wait.

Isa 11:6 sets the leopard beside the kid in the peace of Messiah’s reign.

Usage

"The spots are not paint on the beast; they are the beast — and so is sin in the sinner."

"Quote Jer 13:23 to end an argument and you have used it against its own purpose."

"The leopard of Isa 11:6 keeps its spots and loses its ferocity: grace changes the heart, not the species."
